review_notes: I read the whole target file. I also read ProductMerge.lean and the definitions of productMass, productLeft, productRight and ProductIncrement in VectorBranch.lean. I checked every use of mapProductIncrement and the _map lemmas in TripleScheduleScale.lean and NarrowScheduleScale.lean. I did not run Lean. The suggestions below are untested: I have not checked how the proposed simp lemmas interact with productMass_map or with the surrounding `simp only` sets. The file has only one @[simp] lemma. Its orientation is sound (it removes the map), so it is not a defect. The findings concern missing simp coverage around the new definition, not wrong orientation or loops.

findings.problem: The map has no simp lemmas for its constructor cases (`mapProductIncrement f g (.inl p)` and `(.inr p)`). The only way to compute it is to unfold the definition, which exposes `Sum.map` and the raw lambdas. Downstream proofs do this by hand: `norm_num [Function.comp_def,mapProductIncrement,tripleMiddleVector,smul_eq_mul]` in tripleMiddleSchedule_scale and in the Narrow scaling lemma. The file's own proofs also unfold it, e.g. `simp only [List.map_map,Function.comp_def,mapProductIncrement,Sum.map_inl,Sum.map_inr]`. Unfolding exposes the implementation (`Sum.map`) at every use. A simp user cannot rewrite `mapProductIncrement f g (Sum.inl p)` without that definition-specific unfolding.
findings.proposed_change: Add two @[simp] equation lemmas right after the definition, both provable by `rfl`: `mapProductIncrement f g (Sum.inl p) = Sum.inl (p.1, f p.2)` and `mapProductIncrement f g (Sum.inr p) = Sum.inr (p.1, g p.2)`. Callers can then replace `mapProductIncrement` in their simp sets with these lemmas, or drop it. Optionally mark the definition `@[reducible]` or leave it irreducible-by-simp once the lemmas exist.
findings.benefit: Case-split proofs such as `cases p <;> ext i <;> fin_cases i <;> norm_num [...]` get the constructor-level rewrite from the simp set instead of unfolding `Sum.map`. The normal form of a mapped increment is stated once and used consistently. The three proofs in this file also need less ad-hoc unfolding.

findings.excerpt: productLeft (l.map (mapProductIncrement f g))=(productLeft l).map (fun p => (p.1,f p.2))
findings.problem: `productMass_map` is @[simp], but its siblings `productLeft_map` and `productRight_map` are not. They are the same kind of fact: a projection commutes with `mapProductIncrement`. Each rewrites a projection applied to a mapped list into a map applied to the projection. That is a terminating, size-reducing orientation, as with `productMass_map`. Without the attribute, `simp` cannot push `productLeft`/`productRight` through `l.map (mapProductIncrement f g)`. A consumer must name the lemma by hand or unfold `productLeft` into `filterMap`. The existing consumers, such as the `simp` calls in TripleSchedule.lean, unfold `productLeft`/`productRight` to `filterMap`. They therefore cannot use the structural lemmas.
findings.proposed_change: Mark `productLeft_map` and `productRight_map` with @[simp], matching `productMass_map`. Their left-hand sides (`productLeft (List.map (mapProductIncrement f g) l)`) do not occur in their right-hand sides, so there is no loop. Optionally also tag `mergedProductBranches_left`/`_right` in ProductMerge.lean as simp lemmas so that `productLeft (mergedProductBranches ..)` closes automatically after a map is pushed through.
findings.benefit: The projection-vs-map interface becomes uniform: all three compatibility lemmas fire automatically, so scale lemmas over `tripleMiddleSchedule` and `tripleTailSchedule` that mention `productLeft (l.map ..)` can be closed by `simp` instead of by manual unfolding.
